text: Bandipore, the headquarters of the Bandipore district in the Indian-administered union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, lies on the northern banks of Wular Lake, the second-largest freshwater lake in Asia and one of the largest in South Asia. The lake, formed due to tectonic activity and fed by the Jhelum River and streams Madhumati and Arin, varies in size seasonally from 30 to 189 square kilometres, though much of it has been drained due to willow plantations built in the 1950s. Wular is home to numerous migratory birds, but pollution from the Jhelum River—carrying waste from Srinagar and surrounding areas—has led to a pandemic growth of algae, threatening the lake’s ecosystem. Despite being the richest wetland in South Asia and the largest freshwater lake in Asia, no conservation measures have been implemented. Bandipore is situated on the banks of Wular and serves as a stepping stone to the higher reaches of Razdan, Gurez, and Tragbal. It is also adjacent to the Lolab Valley in Kupwara, just 30 kilometres away via Aloosa village, and upgrading this road would provide a lifeline to the Lolab valley. Historically, Bandipore was a key link between North India and Central Asia via the Silk Road, with a customs and immigration post at Pazalpora now functioning as a forest check-post, earning Bandipore the title of gateway to Central Asia. Strong cultural and trade links exist between Skardu, Gurez, and Bandipore. As per the 2011 Indian census, the district had a population of 37,081, with males constituting 54% and females 46%, and an average literacy rate of 66.53%—lower than the national average of 74%—with 75% of males and 55% of females literate, and 12% of the population under 6 years of age. The region is Muslim-majority, though prior to the early 1990s, Pandits lived in villages such as Ajar, Sonerwani, Kaloosa, Kharapora, Mantrigam, and Aragam, with some families in Ajar and Kaloosa not migrating. The Sharda Mandir at Kaloosa, featuring a rare, ancient tree known as Bran—believed to be several hundred years old—is a significant site. Villages like Chakreshipora, named after Chakerishwar, reflect the region’s Hindu heritage, and the famous Ziariat of Kausar Sahab Afghani is located near Chekreshipora. The Forest Training and Research Institute of Jammu and Kashmir, established in 1905 (originally founded in 1911), is located 3 km from the main town and is a premier body in forest conservation. The majority of the population speaks Kashmiri, with some speaking Gojri and Pahari; Tehsil Gurez and Tulail are Shina-speaking areas with a Shina majority, and there are a few Pashtun villages on the Line of Control. The Kishan Ganga Hydro Electric Power Project, located in Gurez Tehsil, is worth INR 15,000 crores and currently generates 330 MW of electricity for Jammu and Kashmir. A degree college, named after Hassan Khoyihami and established on a hilltop near Putushai village, approximately 6 km from the main market, began functioning in 2005 in the higher secondary school at Kaloosa. Nishat Park in Bandipore, constructed in 1954 under the supervision of then Prime Minister Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad, is modeled after the Nishat Garden in Srinagar and is located on the outskirts of the main market, offering a peaceful environment with beautiful flowers and trees. The town is well-connected by road via the Bandipora–Srinagar and Bandipora–Sopore roads but lacks railway connectivity; the nearest railway station is Sopore, 34 km away, and the nearest airport is Srinagar, 65 km away. Bandipore is known for trekking, mountaineering, and fishing, with Langmarg being a scenic meadow and Arin Nallah hosting exotic trout species. Mount Harmukh, located on the eastern side of the town, is a major attraction for mountaineers, with Sheera Sar (Lake of Spirits) serving as the base camp; commercial cabs operate up to Kudara, after which a 17-kilometre trek is required to reach the higher reaches. To the north lies Gurez, 86 kilometres away, accessible by commercial cabs in summer but closed in winter due to snowfall. The surrounding ranges—Sirandar, Kudara, Vewan, Mowa, and Tresangam—are inhabited by Gujjars and Bakarwals. A centuries-old shrine in Butho village, locally known as Ded Mouj and rumored to house the burial of Moses, is a myth and not historically verified. The Darul Uloom Raheemiyyah, the largest Islamic institution in Jammu and Kashmir, is headed by Moulana Mohammad Rahmatullah Mir Qasmi. Notable individuals associated with Bandipore include Qazi Ghulam Nabi Jan (Chairman Land Development Bank & social activist), Qazi Ghulam Ali Jan (Assistant Conservator Forest), Hassan Khoehami (historian), Siyad Kashmiri Abdul Samad Lone (retired headmaster and poet), Naeem Akhtar (politician), Raheem Lone and Khalil Lone (noted hunters documented in Roosevelt’s book *East of the Sun and West of the Moon*), Nizam Uddin Bhat (politician), Faisal Ali Dar (social activist), Prof. Manzoor Fazili (academician and writer), Prof. Mohd Amin Malik (academician and columnist), Dr. Maroof Shah (writer), Masood Samoon (IAS and writer), and Asgar Samoon (IAS).
